children: One startup is trying to recreate the conditions that power the Sun. Another wants to trigger nuclear fusion using powerful laser pulses. A third is developing a mini nuclear reactor that can be transported to wherever electricity is needed.
Their shared ambition? Turning nuclear technology, long dominated by the State, into an arena for private enterprise.

For Bengaluru-based Pranos Fusion, the attraction lies in making fusion energy commercially viable. While fusion involves combining atomic nuclei to release energy — the very process that powers the Sun — replicating it on Earth requires extreme temperatures and tightly controlled conditions.
“It had become an engineering challenge and no more a scientific challenge,” says Roshan George, co-founder of Pranos Fusion.

A fusion experiment at the Joint European Torus (JET) facility in 2021, which sustained fusion power for five seconds, had sparked the idea for the startup in 2024. The co-founders visited the facility, spoke to researchers and evaluated the available approaches.

They settled on magnetic-confinement fusion, a technology that uses powerful magnetic fields to hold in place plasma — an extremely hot, electrically charged gas. In September this year, Pranos unveiled Pragya, described as India’s first privately developed compact tokamak, a doughnut-shaped machine used to confine plasma. The startup targets its ‘first plasma’ launch — generating and magnetically confining plasma in the Pragya tokamak — in January 2027.
Hyderabad-based Anubal, meanwhile, is developing laser-driven inertial-confinement fusion — using powerful laser pulses to compress and heat a tiny fuel capsule until fusion conditions are reached.
Neither startup has yet demonstrated a commercially viable power plant that can reliably produce more usable energy than it consumes.

For Anubal, the challenge begins with the laser itself. It is working on plasma optics to reduce the size of the optical components used in high-intensity lasers, which are typically large, expensive, and damage-prone. Its longer-term ambition is proton-boron fusion to reduce the neutron production accompanying the more commonly studied deuterium-tritium fuel cycle.

But since commercialisation of fusion power is still years away, Anubal is in the meantime exploring the monetisation of opportunities in laser technology and related systems. The focus is on components and capabilities that have applications beyond the reactor.
Reactor on wheels
Defence technology company Big Bang Boom is pursuing nuclear fission — the splitting of atomic nuclei to release energy — through a portable micro-modular reactor in the 1–10 MW range.

Meant to be transported on a truck for installation at a customer’s site, the reactor’s potential users include industrial facilities, mines, commercial complexes and AI data centres, as well as defence installations in remote locations with limited grid connectivity and dependent on diesel generators.

Big Bang Boom estimates that ₹1,000 crore and more would be needed to develop its mini reactor. It is banking on internal accruals, strategic partners and government R&D programmes for the funding. Co-founder and chief technology officer R Shivaraman says the company targets building a working reactor within five years.

Ravi Jain, Investment Director, TDK Ventures, says  the development of SMR based on fission and fusion are both likely to create big  winners and have a more favourable risk-reward balance. “Fission is something that India understands and has some unique advantages related to talent and thorium-based solution expertise.

In  fusion, the technology development is in the very early stages overall, and therefore teams building on fusion leveraging India’s own learnings can create winners here at par with the world. Globally, TDK has invested in Type One, which is a stellarator-based nuclear fusion approach designed to operate continuously as a clean baseload power source,” he says.
The business opportunity for nuclear-focused startups is chiefly tied to a shift in India’s nuclear ambitions.

The Union Budget in February 2025 announced a ₹20,000-crore Nuclear Energy Mission focused on R&D for small modular reactors (SMRs). The government targets at least five indigenously designed SMRs by 2033 and 100 GW of nuclear power capacity by 2047.
Regulatory rails
The SHANTI Act, which received presidential assent in December 2025, opened the way for private sector participation in licensed nuclear facilities and activities, subject to regulatory oversight.

Meanwhile, the nuclear opportunity has expanded beyond reactors into applications such as medical isotopes used for diagnostic imaging and cancer treatment, sterilisation of medical equipment, and food irradiation to improve food safety and extend shelf life. Nuclear power can also support green hydrogen production.
This opens up more commercialisation opportunities for companies developing and supplying nuclear components and equipment.

Unimech Aerospace and Manufacturing, for instance, supplies precision-engineered components and electromechanical assemblies to Nuclear Power Corporation of India Ltd and its subsidiaries. It is also approaching larger private players involved in reactor construction.
The company has nuclear-related orders worth about ₹87 crore.
Cautious capital

However, despite the opportunities inherent in the expansion of India’s nuclear capacity, especially for the manufacturing sector, the nuclear startup ecosystem remains nascent. According to market intelligence platform Tracxn, only five of the 33 companies in the sector had raised funding — $6.8 million cumulatively year-to-date.
This is in striking contrast to the momentum visible in the space and defence technology sector.

Tracxn co-founder Neha Singh pinpoints the reasons: space and defence companies can tap established public-private procurement frameworks and supply chains, whereas nuclear ventures face long development cycles, high capital requirement, complex liability provisions and stringent regulatory oversight.
The SHANTI Act and government support for SMR development promise to usher in more private investment over time.

For now, fusion startups need to demonstrate that their technology works and find commercial applications that can sustain years of research. For fission ventures, the challenge is to secure capital, navigate regulation and prove that smaller reactors can be deployed safely and economically.

To turn the newly opened nuclear opportunity into a viable industry, private players must leaven their ambition with repeatable engineering, patient capital, and a regulatory framework that gives investors and customers a reason to commit.

title: Founders who chose the ‘nuclear option’
